newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy needs permanent cut in state spending -BOI.
newsitem.headline: Italy needs permanent cut in state spending -BOI.

text.p: Italy has made big strides in cutting its public sector deficit but still urgently needs to bring about a permanent reduction in state spending, Bank of Italy officials were quoted as saying by an Italian newspaper.

"Today the big danger would be that of thinking that, in view of the results obtained with the deficit ... and in view also of the first signs of recovery, the conviction could gain ground that Italy no longer needs structural reforms," central bank officials told Turin daily La Stampa.
The newspaper appeared to have interviewed central bank governor Antonio Fazio even though he was never quoted explicitly.
Italy's inflation has fallen sharply and preliminary consumer price inflation data shows it running at 1.6 percent year-on-year.

Meanwhile the country's chances of cutting the public sector deficit by the end of 1997 to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) -- a key target to qualifying for membership of a European currency union -- have never been greater.
Italy has made progress in restoring order to state finances just as France and Germany have run into trouble containing their own public sector deficits.
Italy's 1998 budget would have to rein back social welfare spending, the Bank of Italy officials told La Stampa.
"Next year the correction (cut) of 15 trillion lire in overall spending will have to involve at least trillion lire of social spending," the officials were quoted as saying.

Under a three-year rolling economic programme, the government plans to slice 25 trillion lire ($14 billion) off the 1998 deficit in the 1998 budget through a combination of spending cuts and revenue-raising measures.

The Bank of Italy was still concerned by the rate of growth in current spending -- including civil servants' salaries, pensions and costs related to public adminstration -- outlined in the three-year economic programme, known as the DPEF.
The DPEF foresees a four percent increase in current spending in 1997, slowing to 3.7 percent next year.
"This increase still appears excessive," the officials told La Stampa.

The aim of reducing spending was to free up resources for invesment. "It is necessary ... to give a hand to the recovery under way, which is still very fragile. It is a young plant which needs tending and watering," the officials said.
The government is currently engaged in negotiations with trade unions and business leaders to secure agreement on a reduction in spending on state pensions.
The 1998 budget has to be presented to parliament before the end of September. Milan newsroom +392-66102321 ($ = 1785 Italian Lire)
